newsitem.title: USA: Weak new-car demand slows May consumer credit growth.
newsitem.headline: Weak new-car demand slows May consumer credit growth.

text.p: Slumping new-car sales helped shrink growth in consumer instalment credit during May, a Federal Reserve report issued Tuesday showed, as auto loans were paid off at the sharpest rate in nearly five years.
Total consumer instalment credit -- defined as debts that require monthly payments -- rose in May by $3 billion, or at a 2.9 percent annual rate.
That was less than one-third the revised $9.7 billion jump in April when credit was growing at a 9.7 percent rate.
The slowdown in consumer credit expansion during May was consistent with other signs of a sharp pullback in spending by consumers during the second quarter.
Government reports published previously have shown that sales by retail stores fell 0.1 percent in May and 0.9 percent in April.
Consumer spending fuels about two-thirds of national economic activity, so a reluctance to spend or to use credit quickly translates into a slower economic pace.

Sales of new cars were weaker than expected in the spring and discounting subsequently has become widespread to try to clear them off dealers' lots. Many analysts think the easing in car sales will be temporary in view of robust levels of consumer confidence about the economy and job opportunities.
During May, auto credit outstanding shrank by $1.7 billion at a 5.4 percent annual rate -- the biggest monthly drop since a $7.2 billion plunge in October 1992.
That followed a $4.5 billion surge at a 14.5 percent rate in April auto credit.
Revolving, or credit card, credit rose by $700 million at a 1.8 percent annual rate in May, the Fed said. Credit card debt had risen $5.4 billion at a 13.4 percent rate in April.

Other credit, the third major category of instalment debt that includes consumer bank loans like those used to buy mobile homes and to pay for education but not home equity loans, jumped $4 billion at a 13.3 percent annual rate in May.
In April, this category of credit fell $100 million at an 0.3 percent annual rate.
Previously, the Fed said overall April consumer credit grew by $7.6 billion but it revised that estimate up.
The Fed revised all the monthly consumer credit figures back to December.
As a result, it said February consumer credit grew by $6.3 billion instead of $6.7 billion as it previously reported and that March consumer credit increased $2.7 billion rather than $3.1 billion.
